## Proposition 3.16
**Statement:** The straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity will fall outside the circle, and into the space between the straight line and the circumference another straight line cannot be interposed; further the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle with centre D, let AB be a diameter of it, so that AB passes through D (D1.17), and let AE be the straight line drawn from the extremity A at right angles to AB, so that the angle BAE, which is the same as the angle DAE, is a right angle (D1.10). Let CHA be the circumference of the semicircle on the side of E, the semicircle being contained by the diameter BA and the circumference CHA (D1.18).

**Step 2.** I say first that AE falls outside the circle. For, if not, some point of AE other than A lies within the circle or upon the circumference; in either case AE (produced if necessary, P2) falls within the circle and meets the circumference again at a point C other than A. Join DC (P1).

**Step 3.** Since D is the centre, DA is equal to DC (D1.15). Therefore, in the isosceles triangle DAC, the angle DAC is equal to the angle DCA (1.5).

**Step 4.** But the angle DAC is the angle which AE makes with AB at A, and is therefore right. Hence the angle DCA is also right, and the two angles DAC, DCA of the triangle DAC are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 5.** This is impossible, for in any triangle two angles taken together are less than two right angles (1.17). Therefore no point of AE other than A lies within the circle or on the circumference: the straight line drawn from A at right angles to AB falls outside the circle.

**Step 6.** I say next that into the space between the straight line AE and the circumference CHA another straight line cannot be interposed. For, if possible, let a straight line FA drawn from A be so interposed; that is, FA lies within the angle BAE, and every point of FA except A is outside the circle. Since FA lies between AE and the circumference, the angle DAF is a part of the right angle DAE, and so the angle DAF is less than a right angle (CN5).

**Step 7.** The point D is not on FA, since D is within the circle while FA lies outside it except for A. From D draw DG perpendicular to FA (1.12), meeting it at G; then the angle AGD is right (D1.10). G is not the point A, for then DA would be perpendicular to FA and the angle DAF would be right, contrary to Step 6. Hence DAG is a triangle, and, the angle AGD being right, the angle DAG is less than a right angle (1.17).

**Step 8.** Moreover, G lies on FA on the side of F. For if G lay on FA produced beyond A, the angles DAG, DAF would be the adjacent angles made by DA standing on the straight line GAF, and so would together equal two right angles (1.13); but each of them is less than a right angle (Steps 6, 7). Therefore G is a point of FA other than A, and consequently G lies outside the circle.

**Step 9.** In the triangle AGD the angle AGD, being right, is greater than the angle DAG, which is less than a right angle; and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side (1.19). Therefore AD is greater than DG.

**Step 10.** Since D is within the circle and G is outside it, the straight line DG meets the circumference at a point H lying between D and G. Thus DH is a part of DG, and DG is greater than DH (CN5).

**Step 11.** But DH is equal to DA, both being drawn from the centre to the circumference (D1.15), and DA is greater than DG (Step 9); therefore DH is greater than DG, the less than the greater, which contradicts Step 10. Therefore another straight line cannot be interposed into the space between the straight line AE and the circumference CHA.

**Step 12.** Before proving the last part, observe the following. Let AF be any straight line drawn from A within the angle BAE. If every point of AF other than A were outside the circle, AF would be interposed between AE and the circumference CHA, which is impossible (Step 11). Hence some point of AF other than A lies within the circle or on the circumference, and AF (produced if necessary, P2) meets the circumference again at a point C other than A; and the straight line AC, joining two points of the circumference, falls within the circle (3.2). Thus every straight line AF drawn from A within the angle BAE falls within the circle; consequently the circumference CHA lies between AF and AE, so that the angle BAF is a part of the angle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA, and the angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE is a part of the rectilineal angle FAE.

**Step 13.** Now let K be any acute rectilineal angle, so that K is less than a right angle (D1.12) and therefore less than the right angle BAE (P4). On the straight line AB, at the point A on it, construct the angle BAF equal to K (1.23), on the same side of AB as E. Since the angle BAF is less than the angle BAE, AF falls within the angle BAE; hence by Step 12 the angle BAF is a part of the angle contained by BA and the circumference CHA. Therefore the angle of the semicircle, namely the angle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA (D3.7), is greater than the angle BAF (CN5), that is, greater than K.

**Step 14.** Again, on the straight line AE, at the point A on it, construct the angle EAF equal to K (1.23), on the same side of AE as B. Since the angle EAF is less than the right angle EAB (P4), AF falls within the angle BAE; hence by Step 12 the angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE is a part of the angle EAF. Therefore the remaining angle, contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE (D3.7), is less than the angle EAF (CN5), that is, less than K.

**Step 15.** Since K was any acute rectilineal angle, the angle of the semicircle is greater than any acute rectilineal angle, and the remaining angle is less than any acute rectilineal angle. Therefore the straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity falls outside the circle; into the space between the straight line and the circumference another straight line cannot be interposed; and the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute rectilineal angle. Q.E.D.

*Remark on path.* For the third part the argument is direct: an angle equal to the given acute angle is constructed at A (1.23), the constructed line is shown to fall within the circle by the second part together with 3.2, and the comparison follows from the part–whole relation (CN5). This is the most immediate route, since it uses the second part exactly as already proved rather than a reductio from the converse of the part–whole relation.

heath_proof_text: Let ABC be a circle about D as centre and AB as diameter; I say that the straight line drawn from A at right angles to AB from its extremity will fall outside the circle. For suppose it does not, but, if possible, let it fall within as CA, and let DC be joined. Since DA is equal to DC, the angle DAC is also equal to the angle ACD. [I. 5]  But the angle DAC is right; therefore the angle ACD is also right: thus, in the triangle ACD, the two angles DAC, ACD are equal to two right angles: which is impossible. [I. 17] Therefore the straight line drawn from the point A at right angles to BA will not fall within the circle. Similarly we can prove that neither will it fall on the circumference; therefore it will fall outside. Let it fall as AE; I say next that into the space between the straight line AE and the circumference CHA another straight line cannot be interposed. For, if possible, let another straight line be so interposed, as FA, and let DG be drawn from the point D perpendicular to FA. Then, since the angle AGD is right, and the angle DAG is less than a right angle, AD is greater than DG. [I. 19]  But DA is equal to DH; therefore DH is greater than DG, the less than the greater: which is impossible. Therefore another straight line cannot be interposed into the space between the straight line and the circumference. I say further that the angle of the semicircle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA is greater than any acute rectilineal angle, and the remaining angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE is less than any acute rectilineal angle. For, if there is any rectilineal angle greater than the angle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA, and any rectilineal angle less than the angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE, then into the space between the circumference and the straight line AE a straight line will be interposed such as will make an angle contained by straight lines which is greater than the angle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA, and another angle contained by straight lines which is less than the angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE. But such a straight line cannot be interposed; therefore there will not be any acute angle contained by straight lines which is greater than the angle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA, nor yet any acute angle contained by straight lines which is less than the angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE.
